1:
The participle divides them exactly. Barnes reads it as breathing out, and explains it physiologically: violent anger is "absorbing, agitating, exhausting, and demands a more rapid circulation of blood", hence "the increased action of the lungs". Clarke reads it the same way and reaches for the same Greek poets — Theocritus, Euripides, Aristophanes — who "often express any vehement and hostile affection of the mind by the verb pneein, to breathe, to pant". Robertson flatly reverses it — "Not 'breathing out,' but 'breathing in' (inhaling)" — and turns the reversal into the sentence that best catches Saul: "he breathed on the remaining disciples the murder that he had already breathed in from the death of the others. He exhaled what he inhaled." Ellicott agrees the Greek is "breathing-in", "somewhat more emphatic than the English": Saul "lived, as it were, in an atmosphere of threats and slaughter. It was the very air he breathed."

Henry, with no Greek in view, reaches Robertson's image independently: Saul "even breathed in this as in his element", and "his very breath, like that of some venomous creatures, was pestilential". Gill calls it a Hebraism and a window into the man — "the rage, wrath, malice, envy, and blood thirstiness he was full of" — recorded "to illustrate the riches of divine grace in his conversion", since that same mouth "should afterwards publish and proclaim the Gospel of the grace of God".

Two notice that yet is doing work. Ellicott takes it for a long interval since Stephen's death, filled by Philip's mission. Henry finds two senses at once: that Saul persisted, "not satisfied with the blood of those he had slain, he still cries, Give, give"; and that "he should shortly be of another mind — that breath will be stopped shortly".

Ellicott and Robertson both report the patristic reading of Jacob's blessing — "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (Genesis 49:27) — fulfilled in a man who gloried in that tribe (Philippians 3:5). Calvin reaches the wolf independently and pushes further: it was "the more incredible that he could be so suddenly tamed", and "such a cruel wolf was not only turned into a sheep, but did also put on the nature of a shepherd".

Ellicott alone reads the visit to the high priest politically. That high priest was a Sadducee and Saul a Pharisee of the strictest sect; but "the temper of the persecutor does not shrink from strange companionship", and the coalition once formed against Christ "was renewed against His followers". Barnes goes instead for identification, naming Theophilus son of Ananus, appointed by Vitellius in A.D. 37 — where Ellicott leaves open "whether we suppose Annas or Caiaphas to be meant".

Henry supplies the biography the others assume. Saul means desired, though its bearer was "as remarkably little in stature as his namesake king Saul was tall and stately", one of the ancients calling him Homo tricubitalis, "but four feet and a half in height"; Paul means little. Tarsus he calls "a little Athens for learning", where Saul took in Greek philosophy before Jerusalem and Gamaliel; tent-making was the trade common among Jewish scholars, "for the earning of their maintenance, and the avoiding of idleness". He dates the change "about a year after the ascension", and notes what makes the case worse and the mercy larger: "so ill informed was his conscience that he thought he ought to do what he did against the name of Christ", and that he did God service in it. Henry's conclusion: "Let not us then despair of renewing grace for the conversion of the greatest sinners" (1 Timothy 1:13). Calvin opens the chapter on the same note — "a history full well worthy to be remembered", of how God brought under a man who "raged like an untamed beast" and "made him another and a new man".
2:
Three stop the narrative to write a gazetteer, and their Damascuses do not match. Gill collects etymologies, among them a derivation from blood — "a cup of blood, or one that drinks blood" — which Jerome joins to "a true tradition, that the field in which Abel was killed by Cain, was in Damascus". Barnes writes as a traveller — a hundred and twenty miles north-east of Jerusalem, in a plain of cypress and palm watered by the Barrady, divided by art into streams through the orchards, "the paradise on earth" as he says the Orientals call it — and cannot settle the population, setting Ali Bey's two hundred thousand beside Volney's eighty thousand. One hill flanking the Jerusalem road, he adds, is called Cocab, the star, "in memory of the dazzling light which is here said to have appeared to Saul". Clarke counts the nine gates, notes the fifteen thousand Christians there "in a state of considerable degradation", and closes on the exports: the Damascene plum, the Damask rose, the damask silks.

Who governed it matters more. Ellicott reconstructs: Damascus had been under Vitellius, president of Syria, but Aretas of Arabia Petræa, having beaten Herod Antipas in the war over the Tetrarch's divorce of his daughter, seems to have seized the city while Vitellius hurried to Rome on Tiberius's death. In that abeyance of Roman control Aretas may have wished to conciliate the priestly party at Jerusalem, giving them a free hand against a sect they would call Galileans of the kind he had been fighting. Clarke and Wesley assume Aretas without argument.

How far the letters carried is disputed. Barnes has the Sanhedrin claiming "jurisdiction over all synagogues everywhere", and Clarke turns that into an analogy his readers would feel: "just as papists in all countries acknowledge the authority of the pope. And as there can be but one pope, and one conclave, so there could be but one high priest, and one Sanhedrin." Robertson grants that Caesar and Augustus had given it, but adds the qualification the others omit: "this central ecclesiastical authority was not always recognized in every local community outside of Judea." He also catches the verb's voice, an indirect middle: Saul asked for himself, as a favour to himself.

On this way, its first appearance in the book, Ellicott offers three origins without choosing — Christ's claim to be the Way (John 14:6), the strait way, or Isaiah's "prepare the way of the Lord" — and explains its usefulness: before "Christian" was general it was "a convenient, neutral designation" for those who wished to speak respectfully "instead of the opprobrious epithet of the Nazarenes". His analogy is from his own century: the term Methodists, "those that follow a distinct method or way of life". Robertson makes it a Jewish habit of speech, and offers an analogy from further afield: "the North American Indians call Christianity the Jesus Road." Clarke notes that Jewish writers designated Christianity by the same Hebrew idiom; Calvin alone renders it sect rather than way.

The women in the warrant draw the sharpest comment. Calvin makes them the measure of the man: they are mentioned "that it may the better appear how desirous he was to shed blood who had no respect of sex whom even armed enemies are wont to spare in the heat of war" — a fierce beast, "as if a madman had a sword put into his hand". Robertson notes that Luke records the persecution of women three times, the third in Paul's own mouth, "as a special blot in Paul's cruelty"; the perfect participle leaves the prisoners "in a state of sheer helplessness". Ellicott finds significance in their prominence — conspicuous enough to be worth arresting — and guesses that among the refugees were women who had ministered to Christ (Luke 8:2).
3:
Whether the light was lightning divides them four ways. Clarke takes it as natural and providential at once: "an extraordinary flash of the electric fluid, accompanied with thunder", but "so modified it as to prevent it from striking them dead", out of which Christ spoke. Barnes refuses it: the appearance is elsewhere called seeing the Lord; the companions saw the light but not the words, "incredible on the supposition that it was a flash of lightning near them"; and "it was as easy for Jesus to appear in a supernatural manner, as to appear amidst thunder and lightning". In its place he puts the Shechinah — the glory that shone at the transfiguration — as "the Son of God invested with appropriate glory". Ellicott says flatly that "nothing in the narrative suggests the thought of a sudden thunderstorm" — then licenses it anyway, since it "does not necessarily exclude the supernatural element" and has analogies at Sinai and Horeb, if the storm comes with "an almost instantaneous quickness". Calvin assumes both: Luke compared the light to lightning, "though I do not doubt but that lightnings did fly in the air."

Clarke's sharpest sentence is aimed at a habit. Many suppose Saul was on horseback, "and painters thus represent him; but this is utterly without foundation. Painters are, in almost every case, wretched commentators." Calvin puts him on the horse: Christ's voice reached a man who had despised it "so long as he sat haughtily upon his horse".

Robertson defends Luke: capital has been made of the variations between chapter nine and Paul's two speeches "to the discredit of Luke as a writer", but if Luke had notes, "he naturally preserved the form of the two addresses without trying to make them agree". The light grows across the three — here from heaven, then "a great light about noon", then "above the brightness of the sun". Ellicott reads the divergences as evidence, not embarrassment — natural "in the records of a manifestation which was partial to some, and complete to one only" — then refuses the distinction: "it is not possible in such a history to draw a hard and fast line between the objective and the subjective. The man himself cannot say whether he is in the body or out of the body."

Both notice the name comes doubled and in Hebrew. Ellicott finds the point in the language: only here does the Hebrew form of the Benjamite name appear, so that the man "who gloried in being above all things a Hebrew of the Hebrews, heard himself claimed as such by Him who spoke from heaven", called as Samuel was (1 Samuel 3:4). Robertson quotes Deissmann for "the historian's sense of liturgical rhythm", sets it beside Martha, Martha and Simon, Simon, and notes the goad proverb is genuine at the third telling "but not here".

Ellicott makes the accusation personal. The martyr's cry — "I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God" (Acts 7:56) — had sounded to the Pharisee like blasphemy. Now he saw the same Son of Man stretching forth his hand, "not now, as He then had done, to receive the servant who was faithful even unto death, but, in answer to that servant's dying prayer, to transform the persecutor into the likeness of his victim." Barnes states the union plainly: to persecute the church is to persecute Christ, "without cause".

Calvin asks why the arrest waited, and answers that God "knoweth the very instants of times": he could have stopped Saul earlier, but shows his mercy better by tying "the jaws of the greedy wolf, even when he was ready to enter the sheepfold" — harder because "men's stubbornness increaseth by going forward". Wesley draws the consolation: "when God suddenly and vehemently attacks a sinner, it is the highest act of mercy."
5:
Three of them stop to say the passage is not there. Clarke counts them — twenty in the Greek, thirty in the English — and reports them "found in no Greek MS. yet discovered", wanting in the Itala, Syriac and Coptic, and dropped by Griesbach as "probably borrowed from" the later account. Robertson is blunter: "the Textus Receptus put these words in here without the authority of a Greek codex." Ellicott grants "a decisive preponderance of MS. authority against" them, then expounds them anyway because they stand in the English text and "belong to this crisis in St. Paul's life". Barnes, Gill, Calvin and Wesley expound them without noticing the question.

The proverb they trace to the same shelf. Barnes and Clarke both quote Euripides, Pindar, Terence and Ovid, Clarke adding Aeschylus — "kick not against the goads" — and both explain it as a stubborn ox wounding only itself, so that the phrase means the folly of resisting lawful authority. Ellicott notes it appears in no collection of Hebrew proverbs; Wesley alone calls it Syriac.

Ellicott asks what the others leave alone: what were the goads? He answers from the biography — Gamaliel's counsel, "the angel-face of Stephen", the martyr's dying prayer, the daily spectacle of people ready to go to prison rather than renounce the name. "In the frenzy of his zeal he had tried to crush these misgivings, and the effort to do so had brought with it discomfort and disquietude which made him more exceedingly mad."

Three of them watch one word change meaning between the verses. At the first, Barnes says Lord "means no more than Sir"; Clarke that it is "merely a term of civil respect"; Ellicott that it "could not as yet have been used in all the fulness of its meaning". At the second, Clarke has it "in its proper sense, as expressing authority and dominion", and Ellicott "now, we must believe, with a new meaning". Robertson makes that surrender the conversion itself, one from which "he never wavered for a moment to the end".

Gill supplies the psychology of the trembling — sins that "rise up like so many ghosts, and stare them in the face" — and Barnes the anatomy of the change: a moment before, Saul acted under the Sanhedrin's commission; now he renounces it and asks what the Lord would have him do. Calvin will not concede so much so fast: "We have Paul now somewhat tamed, but he is not yet Christ's disciple" — still "the question of a man that is afraid". Paul submitted where Pharaoh did not, and not "by any goodness of nature": Pharaoh, "being like to an anvil", beat back the strokes, while "the heart of Paul was suddenly made a fleshy heart of a stony heart".

Why the convert is sent to a man rather than told outright draws the warmest comment. Clarke gives two reasons: "to show that God will help man by man, that they may learn to love and respect each other", and that in Ananias's kindness Saul "might see the spirit and tendency of that religion which he was persecuting". Barnes observes that even a man converted by miracle was still "dependent on a humble disciple in Damascus". Calvin turns it into an argument for the ministry and then a rebuke: Christ sends his new scholar to a man "to prove Paul's modesty" and "to adorn the ministry of the Church", whereas "all men could desire to have angels come flying unto them" — a "preposterous curiosity" springing "from pride and wicked contempt of the Word". Wesley says it in a line: "Admirable condescension! that the Lord deals with us by men, like ourselves." Cyril finds the same principle in the canon, wondering that the Spirit gave "to Paul the former persecutor the privilege of writing fourteen" epistles, "in order that the doctrine might be beyond question".
7:
Luke has the companions hearing a voice and Paul later says they did not; every voice here works on the crux. Barnes answers that "heard not the voice" means they did not catch the words, and points to the crowd who heard God speak to Christ and "said that it thundered" (John 12:29); standing and falling he separates by time, there being "no improbability that they rose from the ground immediately". Clarke gets there by a longer road, laying the scene beside Elijah at Horeb — wind, earthquake, fire, then the still small voice — and concluding that "the thunder must have been heard by all; the small, still voice by Saul alone".

Robertson offers the grammatical solution, then declines to lean on it. The verb takes the genitive for the thing specified and the accusative for the extent heard, so one text may mean the sound and the other the words; but the distinction, "though possible and even probable here, is by no means a necessary one", Paul elsewhere using both cases of himself interchangeably. Calvin reports a bolder proposal and refuses it: some hold the text faulty, the negative displaced "through ignorance of the copyist", but "it is no hard matter to answer it" — the rest heard "a dark and doubtful voice", Paul alone the speech of Christ.

Clarke turns the clause further: the others seeing no man is "a strong intimation that he saw what they did not".

Whether the blindness was a miracle they do not agree. Barnes says flatly that "there is no reason to suppose that there was a miracle in this blindness", and diagnoses amaurosis, sight lost with no apparent defect of the eye, citing a man blinded four weeks by lightning and restored by a second flash. Ellicott agrees it was dazzle rather than miracle, and adds that it left traces: dictating rather than writing, the large characters when he did write (Galatians 6:11), the failure to recognise the high priest, and perhaps the thorn in the flesh — on which reading the Galatians' wish to pluck out their eyes for him "receives a special and interesting significance". Robertson makes it evidential: it "was proof that something had happened to him and that it was no hallucination". Wesley alone puts the scales there from the first, growing over the eyes "to intimate to him the blindness of the state he had been in", and "a manifest token to others". Calvin meets the objection that scales come only later: here "he was blind indeed", losing his sight "that he might forget his former wit and wiliness".

On the three days the readings turn inward. Ellicott places the visions of the third heaven here, outward life suspended while he "lived as one fallen into a trance — in the ecstacy of an apocalyptic rapture". Gill has bodily sight fail while "his spiritual sight was increasing". Wesley marks "an important season! So long he seems to have been in the pangs of the new birth."

The fast divides them again. Robertson takes it as ordinary — "his appetite had gone as often happens in a crisis of the soul" — and Barnes as grief and suspense in a man convinced but with "no assurance of forgiveness". Calvin will not have it ordinary: it "is to be counted a part of the miracle", since even in the east "we do not read that any did fast three days, save only those who had want of victual, or who were constrained by some greater necessity".

Two notice how the arrival looked from outside. Ellicott: the mission was already known in Damascus and feared — "now he came, and the mission fell to the ground. The letters to the synagogues were not delivered." Robertson finds the picture pathetic: "the masterful Saul, victorious persecutor and conqueror of the disciples, now helpless as a child."
10:
Why an obscure man and not an apostle, three of them press; their answers differ. Chrysostom makes it a matter of credit: it was not fitting that Paul "should be induced by men, but only by Christ Himself: as in fact this man taught him nothing, but merely baptized him." That Ananias was "no very distinguished person" he proves from his hesitation: "if he spoke in objection to Him, much more would he have done so, had He sent an Angel." Calvin makes it a matter of who is humbled: Ananias was chosen "that Paul, having laid away the swelling of his arrogancy, might learn to hear the least". Henry makes it distribution — Christ "would employ variety of hands in eminent services, that the honours might not be monopolized nor engrossed by a few", putting honour "upon the heads of those that were mean and obscure" — and turns it on his readers: make much of "the ministers that are where our lot is cast".

Who Ananias was nobody knows, and the honesty about it varies. Gill lists the guesses — one of the seventy, a deacon, a presbyter, bishop of Damascus, a martyr — and dismisses the lot: "these are things not to be depended on." Clarke reports it as settled among the Greeks, who "celebrate his martyrdom on the first of October", and adds that his house became a church "now occupied as a Turkish mosque". Ellicott ventures a conjecture nobody else offers: this may be the Ananias in Josephus who converted Izates of Adiabene by teaching that a man might worship Israel's God uncircumcised — the Eleazar who followed and compelled circumcision being "a striking parallel to the manner in which the Judaisers followed on the track of St. Paul".

Ellicott hears the name, "the Lord is gracious", and finds the symmetry exact: Saul "had come from one Annas, or Ananias, the Sadducean high priest, he was to be received by another", the meaning "itself an omen and prophecy of pardon". Barnes reads the choice as tactical: a man "devout according to the law" would "conciliate the minds of the Jews towards him".

Whether the vision happened at all is where the modern quarrel sits. Zeller denies its historicity; Furneaux calls it "a characteristic of the Jewish Christian sources to point out the Providential ordering of events by the literary device", content with "this beautiful expression of the belief" and disclaiming the facts. Robertson refuses: "that is plain illusion, not to say delusion, and makes both Paul and Luke deceived." He ends with a thrust at the evidence such readings rest on: "one MS. of the old Latin Version does omit the vision to Ananias, and that is basis enough for those who deny the supernatural aspects of Christianity." Two soften it the other way: Clarke glosses the vision as "a strong impression made upon his mind, which left no doubt concerning its heavenly origin", and thinks "the whole took place in a dream"; Barnes says simply "perhaps by a dream".

On the hesitation Chrysostom is most attentive. He notes how the fear is met — "he is blind, saith He, and prayeth, and art thou afraid?" — and defends him by precedent: "in the same way Moses also is afraid", one who "shrunk from the task, not that he did not believe". He is harder on the cause — "God speaketh, and thou hesitatest?" — then catches what the Lord does not say: nothing of the success achieved, "teaching us not to speak of our achievements." Calvin is blunter: "though he know that the Lord calleth him, yet he slideth back, or, at least, he excuseth himself."

Henry frames the scene: "as for God, his work is perfect; if he begin, he will make an end" — "he that hath torn will heal; that hath smitten will bind up; that hath convinced will comfort."
11:
The named street sets three of them at odds over what can be shown. Barnes reports them as they stand: near the eastern gate is the house said to be Judas's, with "a very small closet" where tradition puts the three days' fast and the vision of the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2). Ellicott finds the pieces do not fit: the street still runs to the Pacha's palace as the Street of Bazaars, but "somewhat curiously, the house shown by guides as that of Judas is not in it"; and the burial-ground shown as the site of the conversion lies east of the city, though "St. Paul must have approached from the south". Robertson settles it: the street's line is probably genuine, the ancients having rebuilt on the same sites, but "the identification of the house of Ananias and the house of Judas are very precarious". Most lanes, he adds, "were crooked like the streets of Boston".

On Tarsus they agree about the honour, differ on the emperor. Barnes has the city rivalling Athens and Alexandria, made free by Augustus "in reward for its exertions during the civil wars of Rome". Clarke credits an earlier moment: the inhabitants "in the time of Julius Caesar, having shown themselves friendly to the Romans, were endowed with all the privileges of Roman citizens" — the ground of a claim "of considerable service" later.

"Behold, he prayeth" divides them finely. Barnes denies Saul never prayed, but grades the difference: those "were then the prayers of a Pharisee; now they were the prayers of a broken-hearted sinner", the one "depending on his own righteousness", the other "on the mercy of God". Clarke attacks that grading: "some have laid needless stress on these words, as if they intimated that though Saul as a Pharisee had often said his prayers, yet he had never prayed them till now. This is not correct." He appeals to Paul's testimony of having "lived in all good conscience towards God", and so made "many faithful and fervent prayers"; what is new is the object — "he was praying now for instruction".

Ellicott refuses the subject — "the thoughts which the words suggest belong to the preacher rather than the commentator" — then supplies them, setting "the threatening and slaughter which the persecutor breathed out" against "the prayer of humble penitence in which he was now living", and measuring it by its answer: pardon, light, strength, "intercession for those whom he had persecuted". Calvin makes the praying fill the three days: Christ "doth assuredly speak of no short prayer in this place", but shows Paul "continued in this kind of exercise until he should be more quiet in mind"; the delay was deliberate, the Lord making him wait "that he might the more kindle in him an earnest desire to pray".

The converging visions are where Ellicott meets a modern objection head on. The coincidence "has seemed to some critics, as afterwards in the history of Cornelius, to betray something like the skill of the artistic historian" — an explanation that will seem "short and easy" to those who reject the supernatural. His answer is formal: to anyone not at that point of denial it will not seem strange that "in the work of the highest Designer" there should be "the same unity of purpose and convergence of varied means which rouse our admiration in works of human skill". Clarke states the arrangement without defending it: God prepares Ananias by one vision "and at the same time prepares Saul, by another vision, to profit by this ministry". Robertson notes that "some ancient documents do not have in a vision" here.

Whether the verse is Christ still speaking or Luke's aside, neither will force. Gill notes that "some read this verse in a parenthesis" as Luke's, and keeps it Christ's; Calvin answers the objection, then shrugs: "yet may the reader choose."
13:
How far Ananias is to blame they cannot agree. Gill calls the timidity "the more inexcusable" after the vision. Barnes allows the train of thought was natural, then withdraws it: "when Christ commands, we should suffer no suggestion of our own thoughts, and no apprehension of our own danger, to interfere." Clarke excuses him by the medium: "this was all done in a dream, else this sort of reasoning with his Maker would have been intolerable." Calvin diagnoses without excusing — the objection "betrayeth his weakness of faith" — but insists on what follows: "he yieldeth not so much to fear that he withdraweth himself from Christ's obedience", so what we see is "a desire to obey mixed with fear". His paraphrase is the sharpest thing here: "Lord, what meaneth this, that thou sendest me to the hangman?" Robertson makes the hesitation universal, "a fine illustration of our own narrow ignorance in our rebellious moods", and states the gap in one line: "Ananias in his ignorance saw in Saul only the man with an evil reputation while Jesus saw in Saul the man transformed by grace to be a messenger of mercy." Wesley needs eight words: "how natural it is to reason against God."

Two of Paul's words appear here first, and Ellicott notices whose mouth they are in. Saints he traces to the Chasidim who "banded themselves together to resist the inroads of heathenism under Antiochus Epiphanes"; the Greek equivalent was revived for the new society, since their Master had been "the Holy One of God". Calling on the name he traces to Joel as cited at Pentecost, one verb serving for the Father and for Christ. The point he presses is transmission: both terms, and election with them, pass "from Ananias to St. Paul" — evidence of "the influence exercised on the Apostle by the thoughts and language of the instructor".

On the word's origin Clarke and Robertson pull apart: Clarke derives it "from a, negative, and gē, the earth", making saints "persons separated from all earthly uses"; Robertson derives it from a noun meaning "religious awe or reverence". Calvin argues from the practice: "invocation cannot be without sure confidence", which proves "the divinity of Christ".

The chosen vessel draws the widest reading. Clarke says the Hebraism makes chosen mean excellent, as Jeremiah's choice cedars are the best, the righteous being vessels God "uses, although they be brittle". Ellicott offers "instrument", notes that classical writers used it "of useful and trusty slaves", and allows a second sense — the germ of the potter's vessel, the convert "not only chosen, but moulded" (Romans 9:21). Calvin takes the doctrine rather than the grammar: "if we be instruments, he alone is the author", so that however hard a man labours "there is no cause why he should challenge to himself any part of praise". Robertson makes it four words: "Jesus chose Saul before Saul chose Jesus." Wesley concedes the point furthest from his system, fencing it: "it is undeniable that some men are unconditionally chosen or elected, to do some works for God."

That the call includes suffering strikes Clarke as the whole reversal: instead of inflicting sufferings, "I will show him how many things he himself must suffer for preaching that very doctrine which he has been hitherto employed in persecuting. Strange change indeed!" Lord Lyttleton, he notes, made the conversion "an irrefragable proof of the truth of Christianity". Ellicott finds a motive the others miss: to a lower character the prospect of suffering deters, but to a man "now repenting of the sufferings he had inflicted on others, that prospect would be welcome". Calvin makes it a requirement: "no man is fit to preach the gospel, seeing the world is set against it, save only he which is armed to suffer." Cyril sees the seal that made "the former persecutor an ambassador and good servant".
17:
The first word out of Ananias's mouth is what they notice. Robertson: "all suspicion has vanished and Ananias takes Saul to his heart as a brother in Christ. It was a gracious word to Saul now under suspicion on both sides." Ellicott catches that he uses the Hebrew form Saul heard in the vision. Wesley notes what is withheld: "it was not expedient that he should know yet to how great a dignity he was called."

Who may lay on hands is where two of them turn on Rome from opposite directions. Clarke defends a private disciple conveying the Spirit — the objection that this would degrade an apostle is "a very flimsy argument", and besides "he was not even a Christian" — then presses it into a challenge: "Who baptized the apostles? Jesus Christ baptized no man. Who then baptized Peter? Can the Roman conclave answer this question? I trow not." None but Christ, he concludes, "ever made an apostle". Calvin treats the gesture as a Jewish custom taken from sacrifice, used by the apostles for conferring gifts and for ordaining alike, so Ananias does both — then: "seeing Paul received the Spirit by the hand of Ananias, the Papists are more than ridiculous, who will have the bishops alone to lay on their hands." Ellicott draws the inference mildly: it is "so far a proof that that gift was not one which attached exclusively to the Apostles". Barnes will not call it ordination, "but the usual mode of imparting blessings".

The scales divide them four ways. Barnes denies them: "it is not said that scales literally fell from his eyes; but that an effect followed as if scales had been suddenly taken off", and since the blindness was optic damage, "no literal removing of scales would restore the sight". Robertson agrees on the grammar: the word is as if, and Luke says only "that it felt that way to him as his sight returned". Clarke says flatly, "this was real": the cornea had suffered, its humour rendered opaque, and at the cure "the opaque matter separated from the cornea, in the form of thin laminae or scales". Ellicott makes it an incrustation from inflammation, cites the whiteness that peeled from Tobit's eyes, and reads Luke's care here as "one of the examples of the technical precision of his calling as a physician". Gill leaves the physiology for the emblem: scales of ignorance, of self, of sin, "of pride, malice, and envy".

Barnes still insists the cure was miraculous: no means were used, the recovery instantaneous — "had it been a slow recovery, it might have been doubtful". Calvin reads the three days as instruction, not injury: Saul "is deprived of the sight of his body three days, that he may begin to see with his mind", since "those must become fools, whosoever they be, which seem to themselves wise". He notices too that a man three days starving would not eat until baptized: "he refreshed not his body with meat until his soul had received strength".

Ellicott makes baptism the point on which nothing is waived: "no visions and revelations of the Lord, no intensity of personal conversion, exempted him from it" — and lets the geography close it, "Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus" (2 Kings 5:12) now "sanctified no less than those of Jordan".

Where the Arabian journey belongs Ellicott settles carefully: Luke's straightway balances Paul's immediately, and he puts it after the days with the disciples, before the preaching. His conjecture then goes past the evidence: the Hagar-Sinai wordplay may "trace a local knowledge gained during this journey". Barnes observes only that Luke's silence is not denial. Clarke draws the plainer lesson: the miraculous conversion "did not imply a consummate knowledge of every Christian doctrine" — "without the communion of saints, who is likely to make a steady and consistent Christian?"
20:
All four critical commentators correct the same word, for the same reason. Barnes reports that many manuscripts read Jesus rather than Christ, that Griesbach adopted it, and that "this reading accords much better with the subject"; Clarke is blunt — "the word Christ should be changed for Jesus, as the latter is, without doubt, the genuine reading" — and Ellicott and Robertson agree. The argument behind it matters more: that the Messiah was the Son of God nobody disputed, so what needed preaching was the identification of "Jesus, whom they had crucified" as that Son.

Robertson makes the confession Paul's whole career: "this is Paul's platform as a Christian preacher, one that he always occupied to the very end", and "a complete reversal of his previous position". He measures it against the others: Peter "laid emphasis on the Resurrection of Jesus as a glorious fact", where Paul "calls Jesus the Son of God with full acknowledgment of his deity from the very start"; Thomas "had come to this place slowly", but "Saul begins with this truth and never leaves it." Calvin adds what had to go first: Paul could not teach it "unless he shake off those gross errors which he had conceived of the earthly kingdom of the Messiah". Gill marks the speed: no "disputing and debating with himself and carnal reason", but "as soon as he knew Christ himself, he preached him to others".

Clarke finds three senses in the Greek writers for the verb the amazed Jews use: to spoil a man of his goods, to lead him captive, to kill him. Saul answered to all three. Ellicott and Robertson both notice that Paul afterwards applies the same rare word to himself (Galatians 1:13), Robertson calling it "an interesting coincidence" and hearing behind the crowd's question the proverb about Saul among the prophets "revived with a new meaning". Ellicott catches a tense: had come hither, "implying that the purpose of his coming had been abandoned". Calvin makes the astonishment evidence: Saul's zeal being public knowledge, "they saw no other cause of such a sudden change but the hand of God".

Barnes notes that the word for what he did means confuted but sometimes to raise a tumult, and thinks both are meant: Paul "confuted the Jews, and by so doing he was the occasion of their tumultuous proceedings". Clarke has him overwhelm them "so that they were obliged to blush for the weakness of their cause". Robertson explains the method from the participle, a verb meaning to knit things together: Saul "took the various items in the life of Jesus of Nazareth and found in them the proof". He gives the scene its best image: "it was the most powerful piece of artillery in the Jewish camp that was suddenly turned round upon them."

Calvin, having praised the victory, refuses to overstate it. Luke sets down two things: that Paul overthrew the Jews in argument, "and yet their stubbornness was not broken and tamed that they yielded to the truth, because their consciences rage nevertheless inwardly".

Where the Arabian years belong the moderns disagree openly. Ellicott has already placed the journey before this preaching, noting that "by some commentators the words are connected with the journey to Arabia as following on his first appearance as a preacher". Robertson is one of them: "it is probable that at this juncture Saul went into Arabia for several years. Luke makes no mention of this important event, but he leaves ample room for it."

The increase of strength Ellicott dates rather than describes, connecting it with the answer given to the thorn in the flesh, "my strength is made perfect in weakness" (Philippians 4:13). Robertson keeps it electrical: "Christ, the dynamo of spiritual energy, was now pouring power into Paul." Gill states the plain sense: the strength was "not of body, but of mind".
23:
"Many days" hides three years, and how to fill them divides the chapter. Barnes turns the gap into an argument for the writers' honesty: had this been the only narrative "we should be at a loss", since "it would be highly improbable that this interval would be passed quietly"; Galatians supplies what Luke omits, and "neither seems to be complete without the other". Robertson generalises: "it cannot be argued from the frequent lacunae in the Acts that Luke tells all that was true or that he knew. He had his own methods and aims, as every historian has." Gill fills it from Elijah, where the same words mean a third year.

What Paul did in Arabia sets Henry and Clarke against each other. Henry knows: he "went not up to Jerusalem, to receive instructions from the apostles", but to Arabia, "where there was new ground to break up, and where he would have opportunity of teaching, but not learning". Clarke refuses the question and rebukes the asking: "what he did in Arabia we know not... any assertion, at this distance of time, relative to his employment for those three years, must be both foolish and impertinent." Ellicott speculates in a third direction, on what grew in Damascus meanwhile — "a Christian society, with an order of discipline and worship based on the outlines of that at Jerusalem" — and ends on the sentence that measures the reversal: "from the first it might almost seem as if Stephen had risen from the dead, and was living again in the spirit and power of his persecutor."

The governor who joined the plot draws their most careful work. Ellicott argues the politics from coinage: Damascus coins survive bearing Augustus, Tiberius and Nero, "but none of those of Caligula and Claudius" — so Caligula, reversing Tiberius's support of Antipas, probably made a new ethnarchy for Aretas, whose ethnarch "wished to court the favour of the large Jewish population" and treated Paul as "a disturber of the public peace". Barnes guesses the governor was himself a Jew; Robertson thinks the Jews "obtained the consent of the Ethnarch and had him appoint some of them as guards".

Calvin alone asks whether the escape was lawful, and the objection is legal: "the laws say that the walls of cities are holy, and that the gates are holy. Therefore, he ought rather to have suffered death, than to have suffered a public order to be broken for his sake." His answer works from the statute's purpose — walls are protected so cities "may not be laid open to murders and robberies", and "that reason ceaseth when the question is concerning the delivery of an innocent man" — and he calls Cicero as witness, who allows a man to scale the wall to save the city, "because the laws must always be inclined to equity".

Two hear embarrassment in Paul's telling. Ellicott notes that Paul's word for the basket is not Luke's but one meaning a rope-work hamper, and that from his tone "it had been made matter of ridicule", tied to the infirmities he boasted of. Robertson is plainer: the escape "by the help of the men whom he had come to destroy was a shameful memory to Paul". Three reach for one precedent, the spies let down from Rahab's window (Joshua 2:15); Ellicott adds that "such a window is still shown in the wall of Damascus".

Calvin will not let the escape be heroic: "we see how the Lord useth to humble those that be his, seeing that Paul is enforced to steal his life from the watchmen of the city" — hence "he reckoneth this example amongst his infirmities". Henry puts it as a maxim: "Saul was no sooner a Christian than a preacher, no sooner a preacher than a sufferer"; "where God gives great grace he commonly exercises it with great trials."
26:
Chrysostom opens by admitting he is stuck. Paul writes that he went not to Jerusalem but to Arabia, and that of the apostles "none saw I"; Luke says Barnabas brought him to them. "One may well be much at a loss here," he says, then lays out five reconciliations without choosing: that Paul means he did not go "with intent to refer or attach myself to them"; that the Damascus plot fell after the return from Arabia; that the Jerusalem visit did; that the order was different again; or that Paul simply "does not speak of this visit, but passes it by". His principle is stated without embarrassment: "the Historian for conciseness often omits incidents, and condenses the times." What he will not concede is dependence: Saul came "as being a teacher, not a disciple" — "certainly, I learnt nothing from them".

Why Jerusalem had not heard in three years, Barnes and Clarke answer almost identically, in numbered lists. Communication was slow: no posts, no public conveyances, few roads "except those between military stations". The Herod-Aretas war had cut the ordinary traffic. The Jews who knew had an interest in silence, publicity crediting the Christian cause. Clarke adds that "it is not likely that all the Christians at Jerusalem had been personally acquainted with Saul." Ellicott adds that Aretas's occupation of Damascus stopped the traffic, so reports came "in uncertain and fluctuating forms".

Whether the disciples were right to fear they take differently. Barnes gives two grounds — the memory of his violence, a suspicious three-year absence — then declines to endorse them: "the sacred writer does not justify the fears of the apostles. He simply records the fact." His verdict is a proverb: "confidence is a plant of slow growth." Calvin charges them and then acquits them: the flight "was, peradventure, a point of too great fearfulness, and yet he speaketh of none of the common sort, but of the apostles themselves" — yet "they suspected him for just causes". His rule follows: "every fear is not to be condemned but such as causeth us to turn aside from our duty." Clarke locates the failure elsewhere: they "did not suppose it possible that such a person could be converted", "the full power of Divine grace" being "not yet completely known".

Robertson draws the return as a portrait: "he had left a conquering hero of Pharisaism. He returns distrusted by the disciples and regarded by the Pharisees as a renegade and a turncoat." Ellicott puts the fear as a question: "might he not be coming to spy out their weak places, and in time appear again as a persecutor?" Calvin measures the isolation: "all his own nation was set against him for Christ's cause. The Christians refuse him."

What made Barnabas different, Ellicott and Robertson answer alike, both marking it inference. Ellicott supposes "the Levite of Cyprus and the tent-maker had been friends in earlier years", Tarsus attracting "a student from the neighbouring island"; he "knew enough of his friend to believe every syllable". Robertson calls it "a pleasing hypothesis" and gives Barnabas his due: "it is to the credit of Barnabas that he had the insight and the courage to stand by Saul at the crucial moment when the evidence seemed to be against him." Wesley will not be hurried: "he who has been an enemy to the truth ought not to be trusted till he gives proof that he is changed."

The apostles he met were two, Peter and James, and the visit lasted fifteen days (Galatians 1:18). Calvin finds the lesson in what Saul wanted and could not get: "we must diligently note what he desireth, to wit, that he may be numbered amongst the disciples of Christ. This can he not obtain." Robertson closes: "Barnabas and Peter and James opened all the doors for Saul, and the fear of the disciples vanished."
29:
That Saul now disputes with the Hellenists is where he began, and both press it. He had first appeared as leader of that synagogue's party against Stephen; now, says Ellicott, he "sought to undo the evil that he had then wrought", presenting "the very aspects of the truth that had been most prominent in Stephen's teaching, and which, now as then, roused them to a passionate frenzy". Robertson notes that Luke uses the same verb as for the disputes with Stephen: "it was intolerable to these Hellenistic Jews now to hear Saul taking the place of Stephen and using the very arguments that Stephen had employed. They offer to Saul the same conclusive answer that he gave to Stephen, death." Calvin explains the audience by tactics: the natives "would never have abidden him", so, "being excluded from those who knew him before, he tried whether there were any hope to do good amongst men whom he knew not".

Robertson adds the temple vision ordering him out. Calvin sees the persecutors' side: "behold, again, fury instead of zeal; and it cannot otherwise be, but that hypocrisy and superstition will be cruel and fierce."

Ellicott finds a reunion in the route out: at Caesarea Saul would have found Philip, "the friend and the accuser of the proto-martyr" meeting "face to face as brethren". Returning to Tarsus he would naturally "resume his old employment as a tent-maker" and work outward, which explains why Cilician churches appear organised before any recorded mission (Galatians 1:21). Then: "here, for the present, we lose sight of him." Robertson fills the same silence with a question: "it takes little imagination to picture the scene at home when this brilliant young rabbi, the pride of Gamaliel, returns a preacher of the despised Jesus of Nazareth. What will father, mother, sister think of him now?"

Why the persecution stopped divides them four ways. Robertson takes the plain reading: "the obvious meaning is that the persecution ceased because the persecutor had been converted. The wolf no longer ravined the sheep." Wesley agrees in six words. Clarke rejects it: Saul "could not be a universal cause of persecution and distress, however active and virulent he might have been", and his own narrow escape shows the opposition "continued with considerable virulence three years after his conversion". Calvin and Gill find the cause in the departure, not the conversion: "why was there such peace made suddenly by his departure, save only because the very sight of him did provoke the fury of the enemies?" Clarke and Barnes follow Lardner to a fourth answer, politics: Caligula's order to set his statue in the temple, "to the Jews, a thunderstroke", after which they "must have been too much engaged to mind anything else".

Calvin turns his answer into a defence of men who provoke trouble. That Saul enraged the enemies "is no reproach to him"; Luke "doth rather commend him for this, because he made the wicked run mad, only with the smell of him when he was near them". The application is uncomfortable: "we be sometimes angry with the best and most excellent servants of Christ, if we think that through their vehemency the wicked are pricked forward to do hurt." Nor is the rest permanent: "the Lord granted his servants some short breathing".

On the word itself Gill stands alone. The better manuscripts read the church, singular, as Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson note; Gill argues for the plural, "the several countries hereafter mentioned" showing "that more are designed". Clarke reconciles them: "every assembly of God's people was a Church; the aggregate of these assemblies was The Church" — adding that the word translated rest means "prosperity". Ellicott hears the geography: the book's first sign of "organised religious communities, in the towns and villages of Galilee", though "the history is silent as to the agency by which these churches had been founded".
32:
Peter's circuit provokes the chapter's fiercest polemic and its coolest dig. Calvin sees an argument for the papacy built on the verse and dismantles it: the visitation refutes "the foolishness of the Papists, who gather Peter's primacy by the authority which he had to visit; as if the rest of the apostles did live idly at Jerusalem like private men". Granting Peter the chief place, "doth it thereupon follow that he was the head of the world?" — then the wish that stings: "would to God the bishop of Rome, who will be counted Peter's successor, would travel as he did to animate the brethren." Clarke's remark cuts at Peter, who had stayed in Jerusalem through the whole persecution: "great as he was, he never evidenced that steady determinate courage by which St. Paul was so eminently distinguished; nor did he ever suffer half so much for God and his truth."

Henry describes the office: an apostle "was not to be the resident pastor of any one church, but the itinerant visitor of many", so Peter was "always upon the remove". Ellicott calls this section "the Acts of Peter", though Luke does not "follow the Apostle's course, as in a biography". Clarke and Calvin agree against the English: the word is masculine, so Peter passed not through all quarters but among all the saints.

Lydda they locate. Ellicott traces it to the Lud of the Old Testament, "retaining to the present day its old name as Ludd"; Barnes takes the later history: the Greeks called it Diospolis, city of Jupiter, "probably because a temple was at some period erected to Jupiter"; it is "now so entirely ruined as to be a miserable village"; and since the crusades it has been called St. George.

The paralytic's Greek name, "celebrated in the annals of heathen poetry" by Virgil, prompts Clarke to a rule from Calmet: since both Greek and Hebrew were spoken in Palestine, "most persons had two names, one Greek and the other Hebrew" — Cephas and Petros, Tabitha and Dorcas, this man Hananiah and Aineas. Barnes and Robertson infer only a Hellenist.

Ellicott hears something in the healing formula the others miss: the Greek runs Iēsous iātai se, and in that assonance "we may, perhaps, trace a desire to impress the thought that the very name of Jesus testified that He was the great Healer." What Peter disclaims is what Clarke fastens on: "not Peter, for he had no power but what was given him from above. And, as an instrument, any man could heal with this power as well as Peter." Calvin makes the disclaimer a limit on the apostles generally: "they had no such power of the Spirit given them that they could heal whatsoever sick persons they would", but only what Christ "knew were profitable".

The order to make the bed they take as proof and as poignancy. Clarke notes that, being at home, he is told not to take up his bed but to make it, "strew it afresh, that all might see that the cure was perfect". Robertson and Ellicott hear the reversal: he is to "spread thy bed for thyself, what others for eight years have done for thee".

Whether everyone was converted they read differently. Clarke takes it flat: "the consequence of all this conviction was that all these people became Christians." Calvin will not have it: when Scripture says all, "it doth not comprehend every one how many so ever it noteth; but it putteth all for the more part, or for many". His warning follows: those "corrupt miracles" who "look only upon men, and do not turn their eyes" to the power and grace of Christ. Of Sharon they agree — a plain, not a town, thirty miles from Joppa to Caesarea; Ellicott catches the article, "the Saron, the plain, the woodlands, as we speak of the weald".
36:
Robertson notices what the Greek does: Luke calls her a disciple in the feminine, a late word "only here in the N.T." She is "the second woman mentioned by name after Pentecost", nothing is said of a husband "and so she was probably unmarried", and the deeds were her own: "she did her beautiful deeds by herself. She did not have a Dorcas society." Calvin makes the same point doctrinally: the name disciple is given to a woman "lest we should think that that name was proper to men only", and the order matters — "religion toward God or faith goeth first", the works following.

Both her names mean gazelle, and they enjoy it. Clarke traces the Syriac and adds the custom: "it is still customary in the east to give the names of beautiful animals to young women. The comparison of fine eyes to those of the antelope is continually occurring in the Arabic and Persian poets." Robertson glosses it "the creature with the beautiful look"; Wesley supposes her a Hellenist Jew known by both names. Henry's summary is the best sentence here: "Many are full of good words, who are empty and barren in good works; but Tabitha was a great doer, no great talker." Her head "was full of cares and contrivances which way she should do good"; she "made a business of doing good, was never idle".

On Joppa, Gill and Ellicott collide over the view. Gill reports that the town stood so high that Jerusalem, forty miles off, could be seen from it, defending the distance by arithmetic from Jerome; Ellicott reports the same tradition and flatly appends "though this is not in conformity with the fact", adding that the port was "notorious as a nest of pirates".

How far Lydda was from Joppa they cannot settle: Barnes says six miles, Gill computes eight, Ellicott says nine, Clarke four leagues. Ellicott adds that as at Lydda "we may see the work of Philip as the probable founder" of the church there.

The washing draws two very different comments. Clarke reaches for Homer and the bathing of Patroclus, noting that "the waking or watching of the dead was also practised among the ancient Greeks". Calvin proposes an origin: the rite is "most ancient", so "that in death itself some visible [token] of the resurrection might comfort the minds of the godly" — the bodies washed "that they might stand before the judgment-seat of God, being clean". Robertson corrects the picture: this service "was rendered by the women", though Luke's participle is masculine, "a general way of saying they washed". Clarke draws the plainest moral: "even her holiness and usefulness could not prevent her from sickness and death".

What the disciples expected divides them, two arguing from the same silence. Barnes says flatly that "there is no evidence that they expected that Peter would raise her up to life", since "the apostles had as yet raised up no one from the dead". Clarke reasons identically: "if God did not choose to restore Stephen to life, this favor could not be reasonably expected in behalf of inferior persons", and suggests they sent before she died. Wesley agrees it is "not certain that they expected a miracle". Ellicott takes the other side, the delay in burial suggesting they hoped Peter's power "might extend even to the farther work of raising from the dead". Calvin finds both: the washing shows they did not know, but the upper chamber and the message are "some token of hope" — and he states their wish precisely: "not that they will make Tabitha immortal, but their only desire is to have her life prolonged for a time, that she may yet profit the Church."

Robertson has one more objection, and dismisses it briskly: "W. M. Ramsay doubts if Dorcas was really dead, but why see legends in these supernatural events?"
39:
The widows holding up the clothes is where they all pause. Ellicott identifies the garments — the coats "the close-fitting tunics worn next the body", the others "the looser outer cloaks" — and reads the scene as an institution: the widows were "fellow-workers with her in making them", Dorcas standing "as it were, at the head of a Sisterhood of Mercy". He corrects the tense: not made but used to make. Robertson catches the same imperfect and the posture, the women "pointing with pride" to garments she made "from time to time": "it was a heart-breaking scene." Barnes notices that the grief is particular: "each one would naturally dwell on the kindness which had been shown to herself."

Calvin asks whether Peter knew what would happen. Even uncertain he could not be blamed for going, with sorrow to mitigate and a young church to strengthen; and at Lydda Peter "brake out into these words, without making any stop", where here "he went forward unto the miracle by degrees".

Why the room was cleared draws four answers. Barnes offers two and prefers neither: perhaps "he did not wish to appear as if seeking publicity", since before a crowd "it might seem like ostentation"; or to "offer more fervent and agonizing prayer than he would be willing they should witness". Clarke keeps it practical — that he might pray "liable neither to distraction nor interruption" — adding that "it was not even known to Peter that God would work this miracle". Ellicott finds a memory: Peter had been present when Christ did the same at Jairus's house, and the work was "not to be accomplished by the mere utterance of a name, nor as by his own power or holiness, but by the prayer of faith". Calvin admits the difficulty — it seems "an absurd thing" to shut out those for whom "it had been better to have seen it with their eyes" — but Peter thereby "preventeth superstition, lest any man ascribe to his power the work of God". Robertson adds that the verb is "rather strong, perhaps with some difficulty", setting Peter's solitary praying beside Elijah and Elisha.

Ellicott notices how nearly the words repeat what Peter had once heard: "even the very words which were uttered, if he spoke in Aramaic, must have been, with the change of a single letter, the same as the Talitha cumi" of the earlier raising (Mark 5:41). The speaking, he adds, "implied the internal assurance that the prayer had been answered".

Calvin alone asks why one addresses a corpse at all. It "seemeth contrary to reason", but the reason lies in the grammar: the second person "doth more lively express the power of God in raising the dead than if it should be said in the third". He sets it beside Ezekiel calling to dry bones, concluding that "this was indeed the voice of Christ, which was uttered by the mouth of Peter".

Whether being raised was a kindness to Dorcas divides them, and Calvin turns it into a controversy. Clarke asks it devotionally: her soul had "doubtless gone to the paradise of God", so "must she not be filled with regret to find herself thus called back to earth again?" His answer is that a saint's will is her Maker's, and that "God mercifully draws a veil over all they have seen or known". Wesley agrees that to herself it was "matter of resignation, not joy, to be called back to these scenes of vanity". Calvin hears the same question in a hostile mouth: "brain-sick fellows, who dream that the soul of man is only a blast which vanisheth away until the day of the resurrection, snatch at this place to prove their doting withal" — as if it were "not lawful for God to have respect of his glory as well in death as in life".
42:
The effect they read as instrumental, not just kind. Barnes notes this was "the first miracle of this kind that was performed by the apostles", and "not merely a work of benevolence... but a means of extending and establishing the kingdom of the Saviour" — as when Lazarus was raised and many believed (John 12:11). Clarke counts three results — disciples strengthened, credit gained, converts brought in — "the Church thereby both builded up and multiplied". Calvin lists "manifold fruits" — the poor comforted, a matron restored, many called — then adds what he cares most about: "although Peter were a minister of so great power, yet he keepeth not the men in himself; but doth rather direct them unto Christ." Ellicott adds that the Lord here means "the Lord Jesus as the specific object of their faith"; Gill explains the report's spread, Joppa having "villages and little towns round about it".

Where Peter lodged is the chapter's quiet hinge. Robertson collects the rabbinic estimate of the trade in two sentences needing no gloss: "It is impossible for the world to do without tanners; but woe to him who is a tanner", and "a Jewess could sue for divorce if she discovered that her husband was a tanner." Quoting Hackett, he takes the lodging as evidence that Peter "did not carry his prejudices to that extent", then notices the irony waiting in the next chapter: "and yet Peter will have scruples on the housetop in the tanner's house about eating food considered unclean." His borrowing from Furneaux is the sentence the episode turns on: "the lodging with the tanner was a step on the road to eating with a Gentile."

Ellicott gets there by another rabbinic route: the Rabbis held "that if a tanner about to marry concealed his occupation from his intended wife, the concealment was of the nature of a fraud that invalidated the contract", so in lodging with such a man "Peter must have been taking one step in advance towards greater freedom", having learnt "partially at least" what his Master taught about defilement. Clarke will not settle whether the man tanned or curried hides — "of little consequence" — but infers from where he lived: the trade being unclean even in Joppa, "this Simon had his house by the sea side".

Calvin reads the lodging sociologically, then partly withdraws it. Had the city's leading men been converted, one would have taken Peter in; so "the Lord did gather together there, as every where, a church of the common sort of men, that he might throw down the pride of the flesh". But he concedes the evidence cuts the other way: "it seemeth that he was rather a merchant of some good estimation, than one of the basest sort of workmen".

How long "many days" means neither will guess. Robertson quotes Page — it "might be ten days, ten months, or ten years" — and Ellicott finds "no data for determining the length of time", the phrase covering "nearly three years".

Clarke closes the chapter by closing an era. Here "terminates what has not been improperly called the first period of the Christian Church, which began at the day of pentecost and continued to the resurrection of Dorcas; a period of about eight years. During the whole of this time the Gospel was preached to the Jews only, no Gentile being called before Cornelius." It was right, he says, that they should have the first offer of what was to be "the glory of the Israelitish people" — then the reversal: "when they utterly rejected it, then the apostles turned unto the Gentiles... and thus the reprobates became the elect, and the elect became reprobates." His last word is for the reader: "Behold the goodness and severity of God! Towards them that fell, severity; but towards thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness."
